--- title: "ASM Chapter 3" author: "Alun ap Rhisiart" date: "10/05/2026" categories: [code, julia, statistics, asm, ecology] execute: echo: true warning: false output: true engine: julia --- # About ASM Applied Statistical Modelling for Ecologists (ASM) by Marc Kéry & Kenneth F. Kellner is a fantastic resource for quantitative ecologists looking to deepen their understanding of statistical modeling techniques. It is not as 'advanced' as Applied Hierarchical Modeling for Ecology vols 1 & 2 (AHM), or Integrated Population Models (IPM), but it provides a solid foundation for understanding and applying statistical models in ecological research. It takes a Rosetta Stone approach, with examples in JAGS, Stan, NIMBLE, TMB, and 'MLE-DIY'. But, what statistical Rosetta Stone is complete without a Julia implementation? You could argue the same about a Python implementation, but although I commonly use Python for data engineering and Machine Learning tasks, I never use it for statistics, so I will leave that to someone else. When I read for my BSc there was a course in statistics, and I enjoyed it because it was very practical. It was statistics that let me make sense of the data I collected and draw conclusions. Back then, it was all about using a cookbook, namely *Biometry* by Sokal & Rohlf. Inside the front and rear covers was a table, which you would consult to see, depending on number of variables and type of variables, which type of Null Hypothesis Significance Test (NHST) you should use: t-test, X-square, ANOVA, ANCOVA, etc. Each had its own table for looking up the significance level. It was only when I started diving into Bayesian methods around 6 years ago that I realised these were pretty much all just variations of the same thing: linear models. What the ASM book emphasises is not only are the different frequentist methods related in this way (via GLM), but that Frequentist (Maximum Likelihood Estimation) and Bayesian methods are also related, via the likelihood function. This is the subject of Chapter 2, which I'll write about later. It is not my intention to repeat the explanations in ASM, but just to add Julia to the Rosetta stone approach, with some remarks where I was struck by something. Therefore, if you don't have the book this section may be of little use to you. For those with the book, I give section numbers so that you can match up the Julia code with the corresponding sections in the book. Of course, Julia has RCall, and anything done in the book can be done in a Julia program, combining the speed of Julia for data munging with the exact statistical capabilities of R. I enjoy working in R, but I also appreciate the performance and flexibility that Julia offers. ## Chapter 3 ### Distributions This chapter starts a discussion of the common distributions, namely Gaussian, Binomial/Bernoulli, Poisson, and Uniform. Interestingly, not Exponential, Laplace, Beta, Gamma, or half-Cauchy. That makes me interested to see the Bayesian models later in the book, to see what priors they are using. To start we import the Julia packages, for functions that are built-in to R. ::: {#2 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using Pkg Pkg.add("GLM") Pkg.add("DataFramesMeta") Pkg.add("StatsPlots") using GLM, DataFramesMeta, StatsBase, StatsPlots, CategoricalArrays, Distributions ``` ::: ### Quick Translation Summary | R Function | Julia Equivalent | Purpose | |:--------------------:|:---------------------------:|:-----------------------------------:| | `rnorm(n, m, s)` | `rand(Normal(m, s), n)` | Random sampling (`r*`) | | `dnorm(x, m, s)` | `pdf(Normal(m, s), x)` | Probability Density Function (`d*`) | | `dnorm(…, log=TRUE)` | `logpdf(Normal(m, s), x)` | Log Probability Density | | `pnorm(q, m, s)` | `cdf(Normal(m, s), q)` | Cumulative Distribution (`p*`) | | `qnorm(p, m, s)` | `quantile(Normal(m, s), p)` | Quantiles (`q*`) | #### 3.2.1 Gaussian Distribution The chapter starts with the Gaussian, or Normal, distribution. This is determined by two parameters, the mean and the standard deviation. In Julia we can directly use Greek letters, not a romanised word. ::: {#4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} n = 100_000 μ = 600 σ = 30 sample = rand(Normal(μ, σ), n) histogram(sample, bins=60, normalize=:pdf) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: The rest follow a similar pattern, but note that the way you get a random sample is different from R. There are no 'r*', 'd*', 'p*', or 'q*' functions as in R; instead, you use the `rand` function for sampling. #### 3.2.2 Uniform Distribution The Uniform distribution is defined by two parameters which are the minimum and maximum values over which we want equal probability. ::: {#6 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} n = 100_000 a = lower_limit = 0 b = upper_limit = 10 sample = rand(Uniform(a, b), n) histogram(sample, color = "grey", breaks=30) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: #### 3.2.3 Binomial Distribution A Bernoulli distribution occurs when a binary event can occur with probabilty p, such as a coin toss. If there is a succesion of Bernoulli trials, each with the same probability of success, this is a Binomial distribution. In the book they graph proportions rather than frequencies, and I do the same here. Note the difference from Poisson. Although both deal with an integer, perhaps a count, in the Binomial case there is a strict upper limit. For example in capture-recapture you can't recapture more than you captured in the first place (the upper limit is the number of trials). ::: {#8 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} n = 100_000 N = 16 p = 0.8 # Draw random numbers samp = rand(Binomial(N, p), n) # Calculate relative frequencies (Equivalent to table(sample)/n) pm = proportionmap(samp) # Extract and sort the keys and values for plotting x_vals = sort(collect(keys(pm))) y_vals = [pm[k] for k in x_vals] # Plot them bar(x_vals, y_vals, bar_width=0.4, # Equivalent to lwd = 20 (adjust to taste) color=(:black), linecolor=:transparent, # Removes borders to match R's flat lines xlims=(0, 16), ylabel="Probability", framestyle=:axes, legend=false, xlabel="sample" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: Here is a simpler approach; we don't have to expose the proportions calculations as histogram() can normalise by itself ::: {#10 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} histogram(samp, normalize=:probability, bins=-0.5:1:16.5, # Forces bins to center exactly on integers bar_width=0.4, color=(:black), linecolor=:transparent, xlims=(0, 16), ylabel="Probability", xlabel="sample", framestyle=:axes, legend=false ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: #### 3.2.4 Poisson Distribution The Poisson distribution is very useful in ecology, where we are often dealing with counts with no upper limit and where the events occur independently. ::: {#12 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} n = 100_000 λ = 5 samp = rand(Poisson(λ), n) histogram(samp, normalize=:probability, bins=-0.5:1:15.5, # Forces bins to center exactly on integers bar_width=0.4, color=(:black), linecolor=:transparent, xlims=(0, 15), ylabel="Probability", xlabel="sample", framestyle=:axes, legend=false ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ### 3.4 Linear Modelling of Covariate effects This section shows beautifully how tests that I used to think were separate are actually all related. I must admit that I have never been exposed to design matrices before, and they make it crystal clear exactly what is happening. We start with a toy dataset about the mass of snakes. ::: {#14 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} df = DataFrame(mass=[60, 80, 50, 70, 90, 110], pop=categorical([1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3]), reg=categorical([1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2]), hab=categorical([1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3]), length=[40, 45, 39, 50, 52, 56]) show(df) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

There isn't a direct counterpart to that in Julia, so we make one. R's matrices can have column labels, whereas Julia's standard matrices do not, so we wrap the matrix in a DataFrame to retain the column names. The default DataFrame column names are of the form 'reg:1', 'pop:2', etc so we replace the ': ' with an empty string to make them match the R function output. ::: {#16 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function design_matrix_df(formula, df) mf = ModelFrame(formula, df) mm = modelmatrix(mf) # shorthand for ModelMatrix(mf).m col_names = replace.(string.(coefnames(mf.f.rhs)), ": " => "") return DataFrame(mm, col_names) end ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` design_matrix_df (generic function with 1 method) ``` ::: ::: #### 3.4.1 Model of the mean Next, we can fit the simple intercept-only model. NB: the show() function in this code is just for Quarto, since I'm displaying the output of two lines of code per cell, not just the last one. It is not needed if you have Julia running in a script file. There you would just write `lm(@formula(mass ~ 1), df)` and it would output to the console. ::: {#18 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} show(lm(@formula(mass ~ 1), df)) show(design_matrix_df(@formula(mass ~ 1), df)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}
